warmup.q: A ZGC log line says GC(4) Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 582M(57%)->226M(22%) 0.052s. How long were the application threads stopped?
options: About 0.05 ms in all, spread over three short pauses
Not at all: ZGC never stops threads
It depends on how much was freed: 356 MB takes longer
warmup.why: The 0.052 s on that line is the whole concurrent collection, which ran while the application kept working. The stop-the-world parts are the Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start lines, about 0.02 ms each in that run. ZGC does stop threads, just very briefly, and how much it frees doesn't change the pause.

sections.h: ZGC moves objects while your code keeps running
sections.html:
Lesson 4's G1 log had a young pause of 16 ms, and almost all of it was "Evacuate Collection Set": copying live objects while every thread waited. That pause grows with the work. A service with a 32 GB heap full of cached risk scores has more to copy in each pause, and a full GC on that heap can stop it for seconds. For a fraud check with a 20 ms budget, that is an outage.

ZGC moves objects while your threads keep running. The hard part is that a thread may be about to read a reference to an object the collector has just moved. ZGC solves that with two tricks.

First, every reference stored in the heap carries a few metadata bits, its color. ZGC needs room for them, so it uses full 8-byte references: on JDK 21, PrintFlagsFinal shows UseCompressedOops false under ZGC, and lesson 1's 40-byte Payment takes 48 bytes.

Second, the JIT inserts a load barrier after every load of a reference from the heap. It compares the reference's color with the color the collector currently calls good. Nearly always they match, and the cost is a test and a branch. When they don't, the object may have moved. The barrier then finds the new address (moving the object itself if the collector hasn't done it yet) and writes the fixed reference back into the field, so the next load of that field is fast again.

So ZGC only stops your threads to handle their roots, briefly. Each generational ZGC collection has three pauses, and in the demo each took about 0.02 ms. The java manual says ZGC gives "max pause times of a few milliseconds" and that "pause times are independent of what heap size is used", for heaps from 8 MB to 16 TB.

The versions matter. JDK 21 added generational ZGC as an option (-XX:+ZGenerational, JEP 439), JDK 23 made it the default (JEP 474), and JDK 24 removed the old single-generation mode (JEP 490).

Read its log with care. In Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 582M(57%)->226M(22%) 0.052s, the 0.052 s is the whole concurrent collection, not a pause. The pauses are the lines that say Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start.

try.title: Find the pauses in a ZGC log
steps: Read ZgcDemo. It runs two seconds of the service load from lesson 4 under generational ZGC (it adds -XX:+ZGenerational on JDK 21 and 22), then prints every line of the first minor collection.
Predict before you run: will the pauses be longer than G1's young pauses in lesson 4, the same, or shorter? Will the collection time on the last line be longer or shorter than G1's pauses?
Run it and match the Pause lines to the three red marks in the figure.

code.title: ZgcDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l05; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import workbench.memory.l04.ServiceLoad; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * Runs two seconds of service load under generational ZGC in a child JVM. Prints every line of the * first minor collection, then compares the real pauses with the collection times. */ public class ZgcDemo { static final Pattern PAUSE = Pattern.compile("Pause .*?([\\d.]+)ms$"); static final Pattern CYCLE = Pattern.compile("GC\\((\\d+)\\) (Minor|Major) Collection \\(.*\\) .*->.* ([\\d.]+)s$"); public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(2, 0.30); return; } List<String> flags = new ArrayList<>(List.of("-XX:+UseZGC", "-Xmx1g", "-Xlog:gc,gc+phases")); if (Runtime.version().feature() < 23) flags.add("-XX:+ZGenerational"); // generational is the default from 23 List<String> log = Jvm.lines(flags, ZgcDemo.class.getName(), "load"); String firstMinor = log.stream().filter(l -> l.contains("Minor Collection")).findFirst() .map(l -> l.substring(l.indexOf("GC("), l.indexOf(')', l.indexOf("GC(")) + 1)).orElse("none"); log.stream().filter(l -> l.contains(firstMinor + " ")).forEach(l -> System.out.println(l.replaceAll("\\s+", " "))); int collections = 0, pauses = 0, stalls = 0; double longestPause = 0, totalPause = 0, totalCycle = 0; for (String line : log) { Matcher p = PAUSE.matcher(line), c = CYCLE.matcher(line); if (p.find()) { pauses++; double ms = Double.parseDouble(p.group(1)); totalPause += ms; longestPause = Math.max(longestPause, ms); } if (c.find()) { collections++; totalCycle += Double.parseDouble(c.group(3)); } if (line.contains("Allocation Stall (")) stalls++; } System.out.printf("%n%d collections took %.3f s in all, running alongside the application%n", collections, totalCycle); System.out.printf("%d stop-the-world pauses took %.3f ms in all; the longest was %.3f ms%n", pauses, totalPause, longestPause); System.out.println("allocation stalls: " + stalls); } }

try.expect: One collection prints about a dozen lines. Three of them are pauses (y: Pause Mark Start, y: Pause Mark End, y: Pause Relocate Start) of a few hundredths of a millisecond; the rest are concurrent phases of several milliseconds. The summary shows something like 20 collections taking 0.4 s in all, alongside the application, while some 70 pauses add up to about 1 ms, the longest under 0.1 ms. Allocation stalls: 0.

sections.h: Low pauses cost CPU, headroom and memory
sections.html:
The manual is honest about the price: ZGC gives low pauses "at some throughput cost". You pay in three ways.

CPU. Marking and relocating run on GC threads beside your threads, and the barrier's slow path runs on your own threads. In a pod with 2 CPUs, the GC threads take CPU away from request handling exactly when the service is busiest.

Headroom. While a collection runs, your code keeps allocating. In one run a major collection went 342M(33%)->466M(46%): the heap was fuller at the end than at the start, because the application allocated at least 124 MB during the 119 ms cycle. If the heap fills before a collection finishes, ZGC has to make allocating threads wait. The log calls that an allocation stall, and it hurts more than a pause, because it hits exactly the threads doing the most work. Stalls should be zero. When they aren't, give ZGC a bigger heap or more CPU.

Memory per object. With 8-byte references, every object that holds references is bigger, as above.

Shenandoah, the other concurrent collector in OpenJDK, makes the same trade with a different design. It also marks and evacuates while your threads run, and the manual says its pause times "are not proportional to the size of the heap". Its default mode has a single generation. A generational mode is experimental in JDK 24 and a product mode in JDK 25 (-XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational). Not every vendor's build includes Shenandoah, so check that java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -version starts before you plan on it.

The demo runs the same second of load under five collectors. Predict the order of the "longest pause" column before you run it, and look at the shape of the results rather than the exact numbers: they change on every run and every machine.

try.title: Run one load under five collectors
steps: Read CollectorCompareDemo. Each collector gets the same second of load in a 512 MB heap, in a fresh child JVM. The child reports the rounds of work it finished and the CPU time the whole process used, GC threads included.
Predict the order of the longest pauses, from longest to shortest. Then run it.
Run it again and see which columns stay stable and which jump around.

code.title: CollectorCompareDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l05; import com.sun.management.OperatingSystemMXBean; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import workbench.memory.l04.ServiceLoad; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** The same second of service load in a 512 MB heap under each collector, each in its own child JVM. */ public class CollectorCompareDemo { static final Pattern PAUSE = Pattern.compile("Pause .*?([\\d.]+)ms$"); public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { // child: do the work, report work and CPU int rounds = ServiceLoad.run(1, 0.30); var os = (OperatingSystemMXBean) ManagementFactory.getOperatingSystemMXBean(); System.out.println("RESULT " + rounds + " " + os.getProcessCpuTime() / 1_000_000); return; } boolean oldZgc = Runtime.version().feature() < 23; List<List<String>> collectors = List.of( List.of("-XX:+UseSerialGC"), List.of("-XX:+UseParallelGC"), List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC"), oldZgc ? List.of("-XX:+UseZGC", "-XX:+ZGenerational") : List.of("-XX:+UseZGC"), List.of("-XX:+UseShenandoahGC")); System.out.printf("%-20s %7s %10s %12s %8s %8s%n", "collector", "pauses", "longest", "all pauses", "rounds", "CPU ms"); for (List<String> gc : collectors) { List<String> flags = new ArrayList<>(gc); flags.addAll(List.of("-Xmx512m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+phases")); List<String> log = Jvm.lines(flags, CollectorCompareDemo.class.getName(), "load"); String name = gc.get(0).replace("-XX:+", ""); // "-XX:+UseG1GC" -> "UseG1GC" String result = log.stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith("RESULT ")).findFirst().orElse(null); if (result == null) { System.out.printf("%-20s not in this JDK build%n", name); continue; } int pauses = 0; double longest = 0, total = 0; for (String line : log) { Matcher m = PAUSE.matcher(line); if (m.find()) { pauses++; double ms = Double.parseDouble(m.group(1)); total += ms; longest = Math.max(longest, ms); } } String[] r = result.split(" "); System.out.printf("%-20s %7d %8.2fms %10.1fms %8s %8s%n", name, pauses, longest, total, r[1], r[2]); } } }

try.expect: Serial has the longest pauses (around 20 ms in one run here) and the most total pause time. Parallel and G1 sit at a few to about 10 ms. Shenandoah's longest pause is around half a millisecond to a few ms, and ZGC's about a tenth of a millisecond or less, with about 1 ms of pauses in total. ZGC and Shenandoah tend to use a bit more CPU for the same second. The rounds column is noisy on a shared machine, so don't read throughput from one run.

refs.title: The java command, JDK 27 man page source: collector descriptions

sections.h: Choose a collector with a table, not a hunch
sections.html:
Before you choose, know what you get when you choose nothing. On JDK 21 to 26, the JVM picks G1 only on a "server-class machine": at least 2 CPUs and at least 1,792 MB of memory, both as the JVM sees them inside the container. Anything smaller silently gets Serial. A Quarkus service in a pod with 1 CPU, or with a 1 GiB memory limit, has been running Serial all along unless someone named a collector. Per the JDK 27 source, JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere.

Then the table. These are my defaults for payment services, not benchmark results:

Collector Pick it when Watch out for
Serial 1 CPU and a heap up to a few hundred MB full GCs that grow with the live data
Parallel batch jobs, where total throughput beats any single pause long full-GC pauses on big heaps
G1 most services: heaps from about 256 MB to tens of GB, pause budgets of tens of milliseconds (Evacuation Failure), Pause Full, humongous churn
ZGC GC pauses must stay under about 10 ms, and there are cores to spare CPU in small pods, Allocation Stall, 8-byte references
Shenandoah the same goals as ZGC, on a build that includes it vendor availability; generational only from JDK 24
Epsilon tests and benchmarks only the JVM dies when the heap is full, by design

The flags change with the JDK:

Collector JDK 21 JDK 25
G1, Serial, Parallel -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseSerialGC, -XX:+UseParallelGC the same
Generational ZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -XX:+UseZGC
Generational Shenandoah not available -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational
Epsilon -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC the same

From JDK 24, -XX:+ZGenerational is an obsolete flag, so remove it when you move a service from 21 to 25. The lab turns both tables into code.

sections.h: Epsilon never collects, which makes it a test tool
sections.html:
Epsilon is a garbage collector that never collects. It hands out memory, and when the heap is full, the JVM stops:

Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space

In production that would be useless. In a test it's a measuring tool, because under Epsilon the heap size is an allocation budget: if a code path finishes under -Xmx64m, it allocated less than 64 MB in total, a few of which went to starting the JVM.

The demo runs lesson 2's two ways of summing settlement totals, over 5 million payments, each under a 64 MB budget. The primitive version finishes. The boxed version dies. It dies even when the JIT's escape analysis removes the temporary boxes for the key and the amount, because every running sum is a new 24-byte Long stored in the map, and Epsilon never frees the old one: at least 120 MB.

Epsilon has two other honest uses: benchmarks that must not be disturbed by GC pauses, and very short jobs that exit before they could fill the heap.

It's an experimental option on every JDK from 21 to 27, and the JVM is strict about the order of flags. Write -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions and it refuses to start: Error: The unlock option must precede 'UseEpsilonGC'.

try.title: Put a code path on an allocation budget
steps: Read EpsilonDemo. Each version runs in a child JVM with Epsilon and a 64 MB heap.
Predict which version finishes, then run it.

code.title: EpsilonDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l05; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of the same * settlement totals run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ public class EpsilonDemo { static final int PAYMENTS = 5_000_000, MERCHANTS = 500; static long boxedTotals() { Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>(); // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per payment, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the amount for (int i = 0; i < PAYMENTS; i++) totals.merge(i % MERCHANTS, 1_000L + i % 9_000, Long::sum); return totals.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); } static long primitiveTotals() { long[] totals = new long[MERCHANTS]; for (int i = 0; i < PAYMENTS; i++) totals[i % MERCHANTS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000; // no objects long sum = 0; for (long t : totals) sum += t; return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { long sum = args[0].equals("boxed") ? boxedTotals() : primitiveTotals(); System.out.println("finished inside the budget, total " + sum); return; } List<String> epsilon = List.of("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m"); for (String version : List.of("primitive", "boxed")) { System.out.println("== " + version); Jvm.lines(epsilon, EpsilonDemo.class.getName(), version).forEach(System.out::println); } } }

alt.title: EpsilonDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l05 import workbench.memory.Jvm private const val PAYMENTS = 5_000_000 private const val MERCHANTS = 500 private fun boxedTotals(): Long { val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per payment, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the amount for (i in 0 until PAYMENTS) totals.merge(i % MERCHANTS, 1_000L + i % 9_000) { a, b -> a + b } return totals.values.sum() } private fun primitiveTotals(): Long { val totals = LongArray(MERCHANTS) for (i in 0 until PAYMENTS) totals[i % MERCHANTS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000 // no objects return totals.sum() } /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of the same * settlement totals run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { val sum = if (args[0] == "boxed") boxedTotals() else primitiveTotals() println("finished inside the budget, total $sum") return } val epsilon = listOf("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m") for (version in listOf("primitive", "boxed")) { println("== $version") Jvm.lines(epsilon, "workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemoKt", version).forEach(::println) } }

try.expect: primitive prints finished inside the budget. boxed prints Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Five million new Long sums need at least 120 MB, and nothing is ever freed. Change PAYMENTS to 1,000,000 and the boxed run may finish or fail depending on how soon the JIT removes the temporary boxes, which is why you shouldn't build a test right at the edge of the budget.

analogy: ZGC is a removal company that moves you to a new house while you keep living in it. They carry boxes while you work, and they leave a forwarding note on the old address of each box they move. Whenever you reach for something, you check the label first; if it carries an old address, you follow the note and fix the label so the next reach is direct. That label check is the load barrier. Twice a day the movers ask everyone to freeze for a moment while they check the hallway: those are the pauses. Where it breaks: real movers only slow you down while they're in the house. ZGC's label check runs on every reference you load, all day, whether a move is going on or not.
world: Most Quarkus payment APIs should stay on G1: their GC pauses of 10 to 20 ms are small next to a card-issuer call of 120 ms. The case for ZGC is a service like real-time fraud scoring: a large heap of cached features, a p99 budget of 20 ms, and cores to spare. Check two things before you switch. On a pod with 2 CPUs, ZGC's threads will compete with your requests. And your memory goes up, because references double to 8 bytes. Also check what you run today: a sidecar or webhook relay in a pod with one CPU or less than 1,792 MB on JDK 21 or 25 has been on Serial all along, which is often fine for it.
mistake: Switching to ZGC because "it has the lowest pauses" in a pod that has no CPU to spare, then watching p99 latency get worse. ZGC's GC threads run alongside your request threads, the load barrier runs on every reference load, and if the collector falls behind, allocating threads stall. The man page says it plainly: low pauses "at some throughput cost". The fix is to decide with numbers: measure the G1 pauses you actually have in the GC log, compare them with your latency budget, and only switch when G1's pauses really break the budget and the pod has spare cores. After a switch, watch CPU, pause lines and allocation stalls.

compare.title: Report which collector runs, from inside the service

java.title: GcReport.java
java.html: // log once at startup, and on a timer if you like for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { log.infof("%s: %d collections, %d ms", gc.getName(), gc.getCollectionCount(), gc.getCollectionTime()); }

kotlin.title: GcReport.kt
kotlin.html: // log once at startup, and on a timer if you like ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans().forEach { gc -> log.infof("%s: %d collections, %d ms", gc.name, gc.collectionCount, gc.collectionTime) }

compare.note: The code is the same API in both languages; Kotlin reads the getters as properties. What differs is what the beans mean for each collector, measured on JDK 21. G1 reports G1 Young Generation, G1 Concurrent GC and G1 Old Generation. Generational ZGC reports ZGC Minor Cycles, ZGC Minor Pauses, ZGC Major Cycles and ZGC Major Pauses; Shenandoah reports Shenandoah Cycles and Shenandoah Pauses. The time of a "Cycles" bean is concurrent work, not stopped time. A dashboard that adds up every bean's time as "GC pause" makes ZGC look like the slowest collector of all, the same trap as reading the 0.052 s in its log as a pause.

worked.title: Pick collectors for three payment services

steps.say: Three services, three sets of facts. A checkout API: 4 CPUs, a 2 GB heap, and a latency target that leaves about 100 ms for GC. A fraud scorer: 8 CPUs at 30% use, a 16 GB heap of cached features, and a 5 ms GC budget. A nightly settlement batch: 8 CPUs, 16 GB, and nobody waiting on a single request. Write them down as Workloads.

lab.title: Turn the collector tables into code
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail.
Write defaultCollector: G1 from JDK 27; before that, G1 only with 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB, otherwise Serial.

Write flagsFor with a switch over the collector. Add -XX:+ZGenerational for ZGC before JDK 23. Throw IllegalArgumentException for generational Shenandoah before JDK 24. Put -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions first wherever it's needed: Epsilon always, generational Shenandoah on JDK 24.
Write recommend as the five rows of the decision table, in order.
Run the tests until all seven pass. Then try one of your own services: build its Workload and see whether you agree with the answer.
hints: 1,792 MB is 2 GB minus 256 MB. The test uses 1,791 and 1,792 to check the boundary.
Return List.copyOf(flags) so callers can't change your list.
In recommend, the order of the rows matters: a 1-CPU batch job with a 256 MB heap gets Serial, because that row comes first.

drill.title: Write the flags from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write the JVM flags for generational ZGC on JDK 21 and on JDK 25, for Epsilon on JDK 25, and say which collector a JDK 25 service gets with no flags in a pod with 2 CPUs and a 1.5 GiB memory limit. Then write defaultCollector from memory.

answer.html: // ZGC on 21: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational // ZGC on 25: -XX:+UseZGC // Epsilon: -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC (unlock first) // 2 CPUs, 1.5 GiB = 1,536 MB < 1,792 MB: not server-class, so Serial (G1 on JDK 27) static Collector defaultCollector(int jdk, int cpus, long memoryMb) { if (jdk >= 27) return Collector.G1; return cpus >= 2 && memoryMb >= 1_792 ? Collector.G1 : Collector.SERIAL; }

alt.html: // ZGC on 21: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational // ZGC on 25: -XX:+UseZGC // Epsilon: -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC (unlock first) // 2 CPUs, 1.5 GiB = 1,536 MB < 1,792 MB: not server-class, so Serial (G1 on JDK 27) fun defaultCollector(jdk: Int, cpus: Int, memoryMb: Long): Collector = when { jdk >= 27 -> Collector.G1 cpus >= 2 && memoryMb >= 1_792 -> Collector.G1 else -> Collector.SERIAL }

recap: ZGC relocates objects while threads run. Colored references and a load barrier on every reference load let threads fix stale references themselves, so pauses stay around hundredths of a millisecond at any heap size.
In a ZGC log the duration on a Collection line is the concurrent cycle. The pauses are the Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start lines.
Low pauses cost CPU for GC threads and barriers, heap headroom for allocation during a cycle (or allocation stalls), and 8-byte references.
Generational ZGC: opt-in on JDK 21 (-XX:+ZGenerational), the default on 23, the only mode from 24. Generational Shenandoah: experimental on 24, product on 25.

With no GC flag, JDK 21 to 26 pick Serial unless the JVM sees 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB; JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere. Keep G1 for most services, ZGC for tight pause budgets with spare cores, Parallel for batch.
Epsilon never frees memory. Use it as an allocation budget in tests, with -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions written first.

explain.prompt: Your team lead asks: "Why don't we just use ZGC everywhere? It has the shortest pauses." Answer in your own words: how ZGC gets its short pauses, what it costs, and how you would decide per service.
explain.answer: ZGC moves objects while the application runs. Every reference in the heap carries color bits, and a load barrier after each reference load checks them; if a reference is stale, the thread fixes it on the spot. So the pauses only handle thread roots and stay well under a millisecond, whatever the heap size. The cost moves elsewhere: GC threads use CPU next to the request threads, the barrier runs on every load, the heap needs headroom because the application keeps allocating during a cycle (or threads stall), and references are 8 bytes, so objects get bigger. I'd decide per service from the GC log: if G1's real pauses fit the latency budget, stay on G1. If they don't, and the pod has spare cores, try ZGC and watch CPU, allocation stalls and heap use.

deeper.html:
The full -Xlog:gc* output of one generational ZGC minor collection on JDK 21 has more to read than the pause lines:

GC(4) y: Using tenuring threshold: 4 (Computed)
GC(4) y: Allocation Stalls:          0                0                0                0
GC(4) y: MMU: 2ms/97.4%, 5ms/99.0%, 10ms/99.3%, 20ms/99.5%, 50ms/99.8%, 100ms/99.8%
GC(4) y: Eden              27M (3%)          470M (46%)        233 / 217            1 / 0              0 / 0
GC(4) y: Young Generation 582M(57%)->226M(22%) 0.052s

MMU is minimum mutator utilization: 2ms/97.4% means that in every 2 ms window during this collection, the application got at least 97.4% of the time. It's a better latency number than pause length alone, because it also counts a burst of pauses close together. The Eden row shows the generational hypothesis from lesson 4: 27 MB live against 470 MB of garbage. Allocation Stalls should stay all zeros.

A prefix tells you which generation a line is about: y: for the young collection of a minor GC, Y: and O: for the young and old parts of a major GC.

ZGC also gives memory back to the operating system on its own: ZUncommit is on by default and returns memory that has been unused for ZUncommitDelay, 300 seconds by default. G1 can shrink its heap after a full GC (the soft-reference demo in lesson 3 went from 64M to 8M), and its periodic collection for idle services is off by default (G1PeriodicGCInterval is 0). That difference can matter in a container: a ZGC service's resident memory can fall after a traffic peak, while a G1 service may keep what it grew to.
